34	### Mathematics
35	
36	- Matrix and vector products, the dot product — 1 — he knows only that inner dimensions match; start from a 2×2 matrix times a vector, show that order matters, then C4's shapes: 16×16 (attention), 27×16 (token table), 64×16 (feed-forward).
37	- Rings, fields, additive groups — 0 — no grounding has worked yet.

55	- Steele's talks: juxtaposition, undefined precedence, parallel loops, inference, units, `Σ` over new types — 3 — take as known.

67	- JVM performance: boxing, the JIT, specialization, unboxed doubles — 1 → 3 — where he grew most.
68	- The pipeline, the caches, JVM array limits, warm-up, races hidden by one thread — 3 — take as known.
69	- Loom, the Vector API, Truffle, GraalVM — 0 → 2 — a one-line reminder.
70	- The class loader and its descriptors — 0 → 2 — from his own picture: sizes stamped into a class, as Swift mangles names, so the JIT drops bounds checks.
71	- One-time facts: which phases run the checker, the earlier compiler, a coercion's cost at run time, a load of 30 — 1 — one line when it comes up.
72	- The checker count and the distance to the switch-over — 1 — each time: what each counts, and why one can jump.

75	
76	- Git; Claude Code's client; test-first, with `XXX` tests until a fix flips them — 3 — take as known.
77	- The platform: remote sessions, secrets in a container, the weekly reset — 1 — one line when it matters.

79	- POSITIONS, "History he knows", and his decisions — 3 — take as known; cite a decision by what it says, never by its number.
80	- The coordinator's three principles — 1 — he knows the nine-step form, not these.

82	## How to explain to him
83	
84	- Pitch at a software engineer who directs the work, not a researcher. Say what a feature costs.
85	- Concrete cases before the rule: several, on C4 or a Fortress program. He checks them for a contradiction, then takes the rule.
86	- Frame in what he knows, his own analogies first: the complex-number Mandelbrot, the diagonal matrix, Swift's debug builds, LLVM's lit.
87	- Define each term where it is used.
88	- Show Fortress code as Fortress, infix, not calls. Set notation beside the code. Draw a picture where structure matters.
89	- An ask: the question, context with a primer, numbered options with trade-offs and none that does nothing, the ask, the recommendation last. On types: the specification and the team's later word first, then the library, then the peers as context only. Say what each option does for a fast microGPT.
90	- One ask at a time, answerable as "3b". Show the wording before a yes. Mark a decision surfaced for his learning as one.
91	- Length by mode: three lines and "holding" while he reads turn by turn; an ask 1.5K to 3.3K, 5K with a refresher; long only to establish facts, never unasked.
92	- If he answers a long turn piece by piece: hold, list his points, and wait.
93	- When he's tired: one item, a default he can take, an offer to come back to it.
94	- When he ends "how wrong am I?": answer it, and reflect his idea back refined.
95	- He reads fast and forgets: restate, don't refer back.
96	- Plain words, halfway to ASD-STE100, positive phrasing.
97	- The phone, with Speak: a Select button per section, links not paths, no tables, numbers as K and M. A stop can be an accidental tap.
98	- Dictation: repair a term silently unless two readings differ. Seen, as heard → meant: forty five → Fortify, contact → compact, WordPress → Fortress, Table → Fable, scalar → Scala, Perl → parallel, Docker → checker, time system → type system, rank → rung, net → nat, Sue → Hsu, Popple → POPL, 16 → 64.
99	
100	## Words to avoid
101	
102	- A bare label: "P1", "row 40", "answer 9", "the judge", "the line". Name the thing.
103	- "Closure" for the integer tower; "sealed" for `Σ`; "revising the specification" for reconciling its contradictions.
104	- "Tensor", "reshape", "ravel", "outer product", "ring", "field", undefined; "coercion" for "conversion".
105	- "Yesterday"; "we" for him and Claude; a coda, a slogan, a clever turn.
106	
107	## Open contradictions
108	
109	- Length: he demands short replies, yet praised a long one while facts were being established.
110	- Reading: he says he hasn't read the specification or the library, yet spot-checks them and recalls Steele's talks exactly.
111	- Type theory: he says he knows none, yet reasons soundly about coercion, bounds and erasure.
112	- Scala: he says it earned his Stack Overflow points; most of the account is iOS.
113	- Peers: he asks what they do, yet rules that they only decide between the designers' choices; "context only" is the record's reading.
114	- Ownership: he wants every choice, yet at times takes a default unread.
115	- History: he recalls `main` as free of the third-party port; the record says otherwise.
116	- Other languages: his claims about them are unchecked; check one before building on it.

1	(* MicroGptFlat -- microGPT in native Fortress arrays, data designed after Hsu
2	   (Run C4, the synthesis of rounds two and three: explorations/run-c4/design.md).
3	   The model only: hyperparameters, the layout table, the four vector
4	   functions, the step, Adam and the training loop, line for line against
5	   explorations/apl/reference/hsu-flat/microgpt_concise.dyalog and the formulas
6	   (the tour: explorations/run-c4/tour.md).  The array vocabulary is FlatArrays,
7	   the loaders and the corpus FlatData.  Run from explorations/run-c4/src: the
8	   paths are relative. *)
9	component MicroGptFlat
10	export MicroGptFlat
11	export Executable
12	import FlatArrays.{...}
13	import FlatData.{...}
14	import System.{...}
15	
16	(* --------------------------------------------------- hyperparameters ---- *)
17	(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)
18	(epsilon, lr0, beta1, beta2, epsilon_A, nSteps) = (10.0^(-5), 0.01, 0.85, 0.99, 10.0^(-8), 1000)
19	(corpusPath, weightsDir) = ("../../apl/reference/dzaima/docs.txt", "../../apl/reference/dzaima/w")
20	
21	(* ^T on a matrix and on every plane of a rank-3 array, declared here and not
22	   in the vocabulary because an API cannot declare a postfix operator (row 133) *)
23	opr (m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\])^T[\nat r, nat c\]: Matrix[\RR64,c,r\] = transpose(m)
24	opr (t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\])^T[\nat a, nat b, nat c\]: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,c,0,b\] = transpose(t)
25	
26	(* -------------------------------------- rmsn, sm and their backward ------ *)
27	rmsn(x: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = x / SQRT (epsilon + (x DOT x) / |x|)
28	sm(z: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do e = exp(z - (BIG MAX z)); e / (SUM e) end
29	mask: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = mat(blockSize, blockSize, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => if j > i then -(10.0^10) else 0.0 end)
30	rmsn_b(dy: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], x: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do
31	    r = SQRT (epsilon + (x DOT x) / |x|); y = x / r
32	    (dy - y ((y DOT dy) / |y|)) / r
33	  end
34	sm_b(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], dy: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = p × (dy - (p DOT dy))
35	
36	(* ------------------------------- tactic 2/8: one vector, nine views ------ *)
37	matName(i: ZZ32): String =
38	    if i = 0 then "wte" elif i = 1 then "wpe" elif i = 2 then "lm_head" elif i = 3 then "attn_wq" elif i = 4 then "attn_wk"
39	    elif i = 5 then "attn_wv" elif i = 6 then "attn_wo" elif i = 7 then "mlp_fc1" else "mlp_fc2" end
40	matShape(i: ZZ32): (ZZ32, ZZ32) =
41	    if (i = 0) OR (i = 2) then (vocabSize, nEmbd) elif i = 7 then (4 nEmbd, nEmbd) elif i = 8 then (nEmbd, 4 nEmbd) else (nEmbd, nEmbd) end
42	matCount(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do (r, c) = matShape(i); r c end
43	matOffset(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#i] matCount(j)
44	nParams(): ZZ32 = matOffset(9)
45	view(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], i: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do (r, c) = matShape(i); view(p, matOffset(i), r, c) end
46	
47	(* -------------------- tactic 3/5: the corpus as one padded integer matrix - *)
48	corpus: Corpus = loadCorpus(corpusPath, blockSize, bosId)
49	
50	(* ------------------------- the step: keys -> (loss, flat gradient). Pure. -- *)
51	step(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], b: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]): (RR64, Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) = do
52	    ids = corpus.tokens(b, 0); tg = corpus.tokens(b, 1); vm = corpus.valid(b); nv = SUM vm; pos = corpus.positions(b)
53	    (wte, wpe, lm, wq, wk, wv, wo, f1, f2) = (view(p, 0), view(p, 1), view(p, 2), view(p, 3), view(p, 4), view(p, 5), view(p, 6), view(p, 7), view(p, 8))
54	    h(m: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = heads(m, blockSize, nHead, headDim)
55	    u(t: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = unheads(t, nHead)
56	    (* -- forward, all (doc, pos) rows at once -- *)
57	    x = gather(wte, ids) + gather(wpe, pos); xp = rows(rmsn, x); x1 = rows(rmsn, xp)
58	    (q, k, v) = (x1 wq^T, x1 wk^T, x1 wv^T); (qh, kh, vh) = (h(q), h(k), h(v))
59	    a = rows(sm, mask + (qh kh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)); hc = u(a vh)
60	    x2 = xp + hc wo^T; x3 = rows(rmsn, x2); m0 = x3 f1^T; mr = 0.0 MAX m0; x4 = x2 + mr f2^T
61	    pr = rows(sm, x4 lm^T); loss = -(vm DOT log(pick(pr, tg))) / nv
62	    (* -- backward, one line under each forward line, bottom-up -- *)
63	    dL = diag(vm / nv) (pr - onehot(tg, vocabSize)); gLM = dL^T x4; dX4 = dL lm
64	    gF2 = dX4^T mr; dM0 = (dX4 f2) × (m0 > 0.0); gF1 = dM0^T x3; dX3 = dM0 f1
65	    dX2 = dX4 + rows(rmsn_b, dX3, x2); gWO = dX2^T hc; dh = h(dX2 wo)
66	    dVh = a^T dh; dS = rows(sm_b, a, dh vh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)
67	    dQh = dS kh; dKh = dS^T qh; (dQ, dK, dV) = (u(dQh), u(dKh), u(dVh))
68	    (gWQ, gWK, gWV) = (dQ^T x1, dK^T x1, dV^T x1); dX1 = dQ wq + dK wk + dV wv
69	    dXp = dX2 + rows(rmsn_b, dX1, xp); dX = rows(rmsn_b, dXp, x)
70	    gWTE = transpose(onehot(ids, vocabSize)) dX; gWPE = transpose(onehot(pos, blockSize)) dX
71	    (loss, flat(gWTE, gWPE, gLM, gWQ, gWK, gWV, gWO, gF1, gF2))
72	  end
73	
74	(* --------------------- Adam: three whole-vector expressions over p, m, v -- *)
75	adam(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], m: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], v: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], g: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], t: ZZ32, lr: RR64):
76	    (Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) = do
77	    m' = beta1 m + (1 - beta1) g
78	    v' = beta2 v + (1 - beta2) (g × g)
79	    p' = p - (lr (m' / (1 - beta1^t))) / (SQRT (v' / (1 - beta2^t)) + epsilon_A)
80	    (p', m', v')
81	  end
82	learningRate(s: ZZ32): RR64 = lr0 (1 - (1.0 s) / nSteps)
83	
84	(* --------------------------------------------------- training ----------- *)
85	run(): () = do
86	    println "microgpt flat | params " nParams() " | corpus " corpus.size() " x " (blockSize + 1) " | batch 1, 5 steps"
87	    bsz = 1
88	    p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := loadParams(weightsDir, matName, 9, nParams())
89	    m: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := zeros(nParams())
90	    v: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := zeros(nParams())
91	    for s <- seq(0#5) do
92	        t0 = nanoTime()
93	        (l, g) = step(p, keys(bsz, fn (i: ZZ32): ZZ32 => (s bsz + i) MOD corpus.size()))
94	        (p, m, v) := adam(p, m, v, g, s + 1, learningRate(s))
95	        println "step " (s + 1) " loss " l "  (" ((nanoTime() - t0) DIV 1000000) " ms)"
96	    end
97	  end
98	end

1	(* FlatArrays -- the array vocabulary of Run C4: what the shipped
2	   Vector/Matrix algebra lacks, declared once in the library's own style over
3	   the library's own arrays.  Round two's vocabulary (explorations/run-c/src)
4	   less the block, ravel, vector-gather and validity pieces that the corpus
5	   object of FlatData makes unnecessary; the inventory it was built against
6	   is round three's survey (explorations/run-c3/survey.md).  Views take their
7	   shapes at run time through the library's own reflect idiom
8	   (FortressLibrary.fss:1922-1934). *)
9	component FlatArrays
10	export FlatArrays
11	import NatReflect.{...}
12	
13	(* ------------------------------------------------------- constructors ---- *)
14	vec(n: ZZ32, f: ZZ32 -> RR64): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = array[\RR64\](n).tabulate(f)
15	zeros(n: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = array[\RR64\](n).fill(0.0)
16	keys(n: ZZ32, f: ZZ32 -> ZZ32): Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\] = array[\ZZ32\](n).tabulate(f)
17	mat(r: ZZ32, c: ZZ32, f: (ZZ32,ZZ32) -> RR64): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = array[\RR64\](r,c).tabulate(f)
18	
19	(* ------------------------------------------- the elementwise algebra ----- *)
20	(* One declaration per operator, generic in the index type I, so a vector
21	   (I = ZZ32), a matrix ((ZZ32,ZZ32)) and a rank-3 array share it.  A scalar
22	   times an array is the library's juxtaposition and is not redeclared;
23	   + and - between two arrays of one shape, and + - MIN MAX between an array
24	   and a scalar, are the library's. *)
25	opr ×[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], b: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.ivmap[\RR64\](fn (i: I, e: RR64): RR64 => e b[i])
26	opr /[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], b: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.ivmap[\RR64\](fn (i: I, e: RR64): RR64 => e / b[i])
27	opr /[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], s: RR64): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => e / s)
28	(* a comparison on an array is a 0/1 array *)
29	opr >[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], s: RR64): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => if e > s then 1.0 else 0.0 end)
30	opr SQRT[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => SQRT e)
31	exp[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => exp(e))
32	log[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => log(e))
33	(* diag(v) m scales the rows of m: the Dyalog's v ×⍤0 1 m.  A diagonal is a
34	   read-only Matrix view; the library's product forwards to its mul, which
35	   scales the rows without forming the matrix. *)
36	object Diag[\nat s\](d: Vector[\RR64,s\]) extends Matrix[\RR64,s,s\]
37	    get(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (i, j) = ij; if i = j then d[i] else 0.0 end end
38	    put(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = fail("a diagonal is read-only")
39	    init0(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = fail("a diagonal is read-only")
40	    replica[\U\](): Array2[\U,0,s,0,s\] = array2[\U,s,s\]()
41	    mul[\nat s2\](other: Matrix[\RR64,s,s2\]): Matrix[\RR64,s,s2\] =
42	        other.ivmap[\RR64\](fn (ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), e: RR64): RR64 => do (i, j) = ij; d[i] e end)
43	end
44	diag[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\]): Diag[\s\] = Diag[\s\](v)

46	(* ----------------------------------------------------- transposes -------- *)
47	(* as functions: an API cannot declare a postfix operator (ledger row 133), so
48	   the model declares ^T itself over these; and a call result may not be
49	   followed by ^T at all (rows 144, 158) *)
50	transpose[\nat r, nat c\](m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]): Matrix[\RR64,c,r\] = m.t()
51	transpose[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\]): Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,c,0,b\] = Transposed3[\a,b,c\](t)
52	
53	(* ------------------------------------------------------------ views ----- *)
54	(* the (nr x nc) matrix at off in a flat vector, row-major *)
55	object PView[\nat s, nat r, nat c\](base: Vector[\RR64,s\], off: ZZ32) extends Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]
56	    get(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (i, j) = ij; base.get(off + i c + j) end
57	    put(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.put(off + i c + j, x) end
58	    init0(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.init0(off + i c + j, x) end
59	    replica[\U\](): Array2[\U,0,r,0,c\] = array2[\U,r,c\]()
60	end
61	viewN[\nat s, nat r, nat c\](base: Vector[\RR64,s\], off: ZZ32, _: N[\r\], _: N[\c\]): Matrix[\RR64,r,c\] =
62	    PView[\s,r,c\](base, off)
63	view[\nat s\](p: Vector[\RR64,s\], off: ZZ32, nr: ZZ32, nc: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
64	    viewN(p, off, reflect(nr), reflect(nc))
65	
66	(* a row of a matrix, and a row of a plane of a rank-3 array, as a Vector *)
67	object RowView[\nat r, nat c\](base: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\], i: ZZ32) extends Vector[\RR64,c\]
68	    get(j: ZZ32): RR64 = base.get(i, j)
69	    put(j: ZZ32, x: RR64): () = base.put((i, j), x)
70	    init0(j: ZZ32, x: RR64): () = base.init0((i, j), x)
71	    replica[\U\](): Array1[\U,0,c\] = array1[\U,c\]()
72	end
73	row[\nat r, nat c\](m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\], i: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = RowView[\r,c\](m, i)
74	object Row3View[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](base: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], p: ZZ32, i: ZZ32) extends Vector[\RR64,c\]
75	    get(j: ZZ32): RR64 = base.get((p, i, j))
76	    put(j: ZZ32, x: RR64): () = base.put((p, i, j), x)
77	    init0(j: ZZ32, x: RR64): () = base.init0((p, i, j), x)
78	    replica[\U\](): Array1[\U,0,c\] = array1[\U,c\]()
79	end
80	row3[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], p: ZZ32, i: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = Row3View[\a,b,c\](t, p, i)
81	
82	(* a (docs.positions x heads.dim) activation as docs.heads planes of positions x dim:
83	   plane d nh + h, row i, column j is base[d p + i, h k + j]; and the inverse *)
84	object HeadsView[\nat br, nat bc, nat a, nat b, nat c\](base: Matrix[\RR64,br,bc\], p: ZZ32, nh: ZZ32, k: ZZ32)
85	        extends Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\]
86	    get(ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (q, i, j) = ix; base.get((q DIV nh) p + i, (q MOD nh) k + j) end
87	    put(ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (q, i, j) = ix; base.put(((q DIV nh) p + i, (q MOD nh) k + j), x) end
88	    init0(ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (q, i, j) = ix; base.init0(((q DIV nh) p + i, (q MOD nh) k + j), x) end
89	    replica[\U\](): Array3[\U,0,a,0,b,0,c\] = array3[\U,a,b,c\]()
90	end
91	headsN[\nat br, nat bc, nat a, nat b, nat c\](base: Matrix[\RR64,br,bc\], p: ZZ32, nh: ZZ32, k: ZZ32, _: N[\a\], _: N[\b\], _: N[\c\]): Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\] =
92	    HeadsView[\br,bc,a,b,c\](base, p, nh, k)
93	heads[\nat br, nat bc\](base: Matrix[\RR64,br,bc\], p: ZZ32, nh: ZZ32, k: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
94	    (nr, nc) = base.sizes
95	    headsN(base, p, nh, k, reflect((nr DIV p) nh), reflect(p), reflect(k))
96	  end
97	object UnheadsView[\nat a, nat b, nat c, nat r, nat cc\](base: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], nh: ZZ32)
98	        extends Matrix[\RR64,r,cc\]
99	    get(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (i, j) = ij; base.get(((i DIV b) nh + (j DIV c), i MOD b, j MOD c)) end
100	    put(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.put(((i DIV b) nh + (j DIV c), i MOD b, j MOD c), x) end
101	    init0(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.init0(((i DIV b) nh + (j DIV c), i MOD b, j MOD c), x) end
102	    replica[\U\](): Array2[\U,0,r,0,cc\] = array2[\U,r,cc\]()
103	end
104	unheadsN[\nat a, nat b, nat c, nat r, nat cc\](base: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], nh: ZZ32, _: N[\r\], _: N[\cc\]): Matrix[\RR64,r,cc\] =
105	    UnheadsView[\a,b,c,r,cc\](base, nh)
106	unheads[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], nh: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
107	    (np, p, k) = t.sizes
108	    unheadsN(t, nh, reflect((np DIV nh) p), reflect(nh k))
109	  end
110	(* a plane of a rank-3 array as a matrix, and every plane transposed *)
111	object PlaneView[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](base: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], p: ZZ32) extends Matrix[\RR64,b,c\]
112	    get(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (i, j) = ij; base.get((p, i, j)) end
113	    put(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.put((p, i, j), x) end
114	    init0(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.init0((p, i, j), x) end
115	    replica[\U\](): Array2[\U,0,b,0,c\] = array2[\U,b,c\]()
116	end
117	plane[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], p: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = PlaneView[\a,b,c\](t, p)
118	object Transposed3[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](base: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\]) extends Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,c,0,b\]
119	    get(ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (p, i, j) = ix; base.get((p, j, i)) end
120	    put(ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (p, i, j) = ix; base.put((p, j, i), x) end
121	    init0(ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (p, i, j) = ix; base.init0((p, j, i), x) end
122	    replica[\U\](): Array3[\U,0,a,0,c,0,b\] = array3[\U,a,c,b\]()
123	end

125	(* ------------------------------------------------- rank-3 algebra -------- *)
126	(* +.×⍤2 : the library product on every pair of planes *)
127	opr juxtaposition[\nat a, nat b, nat c, nat a2, nat b2, nat c2\](x: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], y: Array3[\RR64,0,a2,0,b2,0,c2\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
128	    (np, n, d) = x.sizes
129	    (yp, yn, yd) = y.sizes
130	    out = array[\RR64\](np, n, yd)
131	    for p <- 0#np do (plane(out, p)).assign((plane(x, p)) (plane(y, p))) end
132	    out
133	  end
134	(* m +⍤2 t : a matrix added to every plane *)
135	opr +[\nat r, nat c, nat a, nat b, nat d\](m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\], t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,d\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
136	    t.ivmap[\RR64\](fn (ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32), e: RR64): RR64 => do (p, i, j) = ix; m[i,j] + e end)
137	
138	(* -------------------------------------------------- the row lift --------- *)
139	(* f⍤1 : f on every row of m, the results stacked; the dyadic form pairs the
140	   rows of two matrices; over a rank-3 array the rows are those of every plane.
141	   A parallel for over the rows, each written through a row view. *)
142	rows[\nat r, nat c\](f: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] -> Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
143	    (n, d) = m.sizes
144	    out = array[\RR64\](n, d)
145	    for i <- 0#n do (row(out, i)).assign(f(row(m, i))) end
146	    out
147	  end
148	rows[\nat r, nat c, nat r2, nat c2\](f: (Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) -> Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], x: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\], y: Matrix[\RR64,r2,c2\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
149	    (n, d) = x.sizes
150	    out = array[\RR64\](n, d)
151	    for i <- 0#n do (row(out, i)).assign(f(row(x, i), row(y, i))) end
152	    out
153	  end
154	rows[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](f: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] -> Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
155	    (np, n, d) = t.sizes
156	    out = array[\RR64\](np, n, d)
157	    for p <- 0#np, i <- 0#n do (row3(out, p, i)).assign(f(row3(t, p, i))) end
158	    out
159	  end
160	rows[\nat a, nat b, nat c, nat a2, nat b2, nat c2\](f: (Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) -> Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], x: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], y: Array3[\RR64,0,a2,0,b2,0,c2\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
161	    (np, n, d) = x.sizes
162	    out = array[\RR64\](np, n, d)
163	    for p <- 0#np, i <- 0#n do (row3(out, p, i)).assign(f(row3(x, p, i), row3(y, p, i))) end
164	    out
165	  end
166	
167	(* ----------------------------------------------------------- keys -------- *)
168	(* the rows of m at the keys: m[ks;]; the elements of v at the keys: v[ks] *)
169	gather[\T extends Number, nat r, nat c, nat k\](m: Matrix[\T,r,c\], ks: Vector[\ZZ32,k\]): Array[\T,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
170	    (nr, nc) = m.sizes
171	    array[\T\](|ks|, nc).tabulate(fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): T => m[ks[i], j])
172	  end
173	(* ks ∘.= ⍳width, as 0/1 *)
174	onehot[\nat k\](ks: Vector[\ZZ32,k\], width: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
175	    mat(|ks|, width, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => if ks[i] = j then 1.0 else 0.0 end)
176	(* ks ⌷⍤0 1 m : element ks[i] of row i *)
177	pick[\nat r, nat c, nat k\](m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\], ks: Vector[\ZZ32,k\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] =
178	    vec(|ks|, fn (i: ZZ32): RR64 => m[i, ks[i]])
179	(* ⊃,/,¨ : the matrices ravelled and catenated into one vector, in order *)
180	flat(ms: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]...): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do
181	    out = zeros(SUM[\ZZ32\][m <- ms] |m|)
182	    off: ZZ32 := 0
183	    for m <- seq(ms) do
184	        (nr, nc) = m.sizes
185	        for i <- 0#nr, j <- 0#nc do out[off + i nc + j] := m[i,j] end
186	        off += nr nc
187	    end
188	    out
189	  end
190	end

1	(* FlatData -- the loaders and the corpus for MicroGptFlat (Run C4).
2	   The weights are nine text files, one matrix row per line, read straight
3	   into one flat vector in layout order; the corpus is one padded integer
4	   matrix (documents x block+1) with a length per document (Hsu's tactics
5	   3 and 5). The float parser is here because the library's strToFloat
6	   mis-parses a sign and overflows on a 17-digit mantissa (ledger row 140)
7	   and String.split is not a tokenizer (row 141). *)
8	component FlatData
9	export FlatData
10	import FlatArrays.{...}
11	import File.{...}
12	
13	(* decimal digits, optional '.', optional e/E exponent; leading '-' or '¯' *)
14	parseFloat(s: String): RR64 = do
15	    neg = (s[0] = '-') OR (s[0] = '¯')
16	    m: RR64 := 0.0
17	    scale: ZZ32 := 0
18	    ex: ZZ32 := 0
19	    i: ZZ32 := if neg then 1 else 0 end
20	    seenPoint: Boolean := false
21	    n = |s|
22	    while (i < n) AND: ((s[i] =/= 'e') AND (s[i] =/= 'E')) do
23	        c = s[i]
24	        if c = '.' then seenPoint := true
25	        else
26	            m := 10.0 m + (c.codePoint - '0'.codePoint)
27	            if seenPoint then scale += 1 end
28	        end
29	        i += 1
30	    end
31	    if i < n then
32	        eneg = (s[i+1] = '-') OR (s[i+1] = '¯')
33	        j = if eneg OR (s[i+1] = '+') then i + 2 else i + 1 end
34	        ex := strToInt(s[j # (n - j)])
35	        if eneg then ex := -ex end
36	    end
37	    e10 = ex - scale
38	    r = if e10 >= 0 then m (10.0^e10)
39	        elif e10 >= -22 then m / (10.0^(-e10))
40	        else (m / (10.0^22)) / (10.0^(-e10 - 22)) end
41	    if neg then -r else r end
42	  end
43	
44	(* the space-separated numbers of a line, into out[off..]; returns how many *)
45	parseRow[\nat s\](line: String, out: Vector[\RR64,s\], off: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do
46	    n = |line|
47	    i: ZZ32 := 0
48	    k: ZZ32 := 0
49	    while i < n do
50	        if line[i] = ' ' then i += 1
51	        else
52	            j: ZZ32 := i
53	            while (j < n) AND: (line[j] =/= ' ') do j += 1 end
54	            out[off + k] := parseFloat(line[i # (j - i)])
55	            k += 1
56	            i := j
57	        end
58	    end
59	    k
60	  end
61	(* the numbers of a line as a vector (two scans: count, then fill) *)
62	numbersOf(line: String): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do
63	    cnt = parseRow(line, zeros(|line|), 0)
64	    out = zeros(cnt)
65	    parseRow(line, out, 0)
66	    out
67	  end
68	(* the lines of a file, up to the first empty one *)
69	readLines(path: String): Array[\String,ZZ32\] = do
70	    f = FileReadStream(path)
71	    cnt: ZZ32 := 0
72	    line: String := f.readLine()
73	    while |line| > 0 do cnt += 1; line := f.readLine() end
74	    f.close()
75	    g = FileReadStream(path)
76	    out = array[\String\](cnt).fill("")
77	    for i <- seq(0#cnt) do out[i] := g.readLine() end
78	    g.close()
79	    out
80	  end
81	(* one number per line *)
82	readVector(path: String, n: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do
83	    f = FileReadStream(path)
84	    v = zeros(n)
85	    for i <- seq(0#n) do v[i] := parseFloat(f.readLine()) end
86	    f.close()
87	    v
88	  end
89	
90	(* the weights: files name(0) .. name(count-1) under dir, every line's numbers
91	   appended in order into one vector of `total` values -- the layout is the
92	   caller's table, the loader only concatenates *)
93	loadParams(dir: String, name: ZZ32 -> String, count: ZZ32, total: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do
94	    p = zeros(total)
95	    off: ZZ32 := 0
96	    for i <- seq(0#count) do
97	        for line <- seq(readLines(dir "/" name(i) ".txt")) do off += parseRow(line, p, off) end
98	    end
99	    if off =/= total then fail("loaded " off " numbers, the layout has " total) end
100	    p
101	  end
102	
103	(* the corpus: one document per line, interned a..z; the token matrix has
104	   width block+1, BOS before and after each document and in every unused
105	   slot, and a length per document (its characters plus the leading BOS) *)
106	object Corpus(tokm: Array[\ZZ32,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\], len: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\], blk: ZZ32)
107	    size(): ZZ32 = |len|
108	    length(d: ZZ32): ZZ32 = len[d]
109	    token(d: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): ZZ32 = tokm[d, j]
110	    (* the keys of a batch b of documents, one row per (document, position):
111	       the tokens at position + off, the positions, and the 0/1 validity mask *)
112	    tokens(b: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\], off: ZZ32): Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\] =
113	        keys(|b| blk, fn (r: ZZ32): ZZ32 => tokm[b[r DIV blk], (r MOD blk) + off])
114	    positions(b: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]): Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\] =
115	        keys(|b| blk, fn (r: ZZ32): ZZ32 => r MOD blk)
116	    valid(b: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] =
117	        vec(|b| blk, fn (r: ZZ32): RR64 => if (r MOD blk) < len[b[r DIV blk]] then 1.0 else 0.0 end)
118	end
119	loadCorpus(path: String, blk: ZZ32, bos: ZZ32): Corpus = do
120	    names = readLines(path)
121	    tokm = array[\ZZ32\](|names|, blk + 1).fill(bos)
122	    for d <- seq(0#|names|), j <- seq(0#|names[d]|) do tokm[d, 1 + j] := names[d][j].codePoint - 'a'.codePoint end
123	    Corpus(tokm, keys(|names|, fn (d: ZZ32): ZZ32 => 1 + |names[d]|), blk)
124	  end
125	end

1	(* MicroGptFlatQuick -- the quick check of Run C4's model: the first two steps of
2	   MicroGptFlatCheck's batch 1 (documents 0 and 1 from the committed weights,
3	   one Adam step between them), two forward-and-backward passes in all, with
4	   its loader and corpus checks, 7 checks against the same goldens of Run C
5	   (explorations/run-c/goldens): the step-1 loss, the step-0 gradient and its
6	   zero entries, the parameters after Adam, and the step-2 loss on the updated
7	   parameters.  One line per check with the measured difference and PASS or
8	   FAIL, then an aggregate verdict; any FAIL ends the run with a non-zero
9	   status.  The full 40 checks: MicroGptFlatCheck.fss beside it.
10	   Run from explorations/run-c4/src:  ../../../bin/fortress MicroGptFlatQuick.fss *)
11	component MicroGptFlatQuick
12	export Executable
13	import MicroGptFlat.{...}
14	import FlatArrays.{...}
15	import FlatData.{...}
16	import System.{...}
17	
18	goldensDir: String = "../../run-c/goldens"
19	tolLoss: RR64 = 10.0^(-12)
20	tolGrad: RR64 = 10.0^(-12)
21	
22	passed: ZZ32 := 0
23	failed: ZZ32 := 0
24	report(name: String, diff: RR64, tol: RR64): () = do
25	    ok = diff <= tol
26	    if ok then passed += 1 else failed += 1 end
27	    println name ": diff " diff " " (if ok then "PASS" else "FAIL" end)
28	  end
29	maxAbsDiff(a: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], b: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): RR64 = BIG MAX[\RR64\][i <- 0#|a|] |a[i] - b[i]|
30	
31	run(): () = do
32	    println "MicroGptFlat quick checks (Run C4, two steps) | threads " (getProperty("fortress.threads", "?")) " | tolerances: loss " tolLoss " grad " tolGrad
33	    wall0 = nanoTime()
34	    p0 = loadParams("../../apl/reference/dzaima/w", matName, 9, nParams())
35	    (* 0. the loaders against the goldens' P0 and corpus rows *)
36	    report("loader: max |P - P0| over 4192", maxAbsDiff(p0, readVector(goldensDir "/P0.txt", 4192)), 0.0)
37	    lines = readLines(goldensDir "/corpus_first16.txt")
38	    corpusDiff = BIG MAX[\RR64\][d <- 0#16] do
39	        nums = numbersOf(lines[d].beyond(' '))   (* the line is: name len t0 .. t16; nums[0] is len *)
40	        (BIG MAX[\RR64\][j <- 0#17] |nums[1 + j] - (1.0 corpus.token(d, j))|) MAX |nums[0] - (1.0 corpus.length(d))|
41	      end
42	    report("corpus: max |row - golden| over documents 0..15", corpusDiff, 0.0)
43	    (* 1. batch 1, the first two of the full check's five Adam steps, on documents 0 and 1 *)
44	    losses = readVector(goldensDir "/losses_batch1_5steps.txt", 5)
45	    t0 = nanoTime()
46	    (l0, g0) = step(p0, keys(1, fn (i: ZZ32): ZZ32 => 0))
47	    report("batch 1 step 1 loss " l0 " vs " losses[0] " (" ((nanoTime() - t0) DIV 1000000) " ms)", |l0 - losses[0]|, tolLoss)
48	    report("step 0 batch 1: max |gradient - golden| over 4192", maxAbsDiff(g0, readVector(goldensDir "/grad_step0.txt", 4192)), tolGrad)
49	    zeroCount = SUM[\ZZ32\][i <- 0#nParams()] (if g0[i] = 0.0 then 1 else 0 end)
50	    report("step 0 batch 1: zero gradient entries - 464", |1.0 zeroCount - 464.0|, 0.0)
51	    (p1, m1, v1) = adam(p0, zeros(nParams()), zeros(nParams()), g0, 1, learningRate(0))
52	    report("step 0 batch 1: max |P after Adam - golden| over 4192", maxAbsDiff(p1, readVector(goldensDir "/P_after_adam.txt", 4192)), tolGrad)
53	    t1 = nanoTime()
54	    (l1, g1) = step(p1, keys(1, fn (i: ZZ32): ZZ32 => 1))
55	    report("batch 1 step 2 loss " l1 " vs " losses[1] " (" ((nanoTime() - t1) DIV 1000000) " ms)", |l1 - losses[1]|, tolLoss)
56	    println "total " ((nanoTime() - wall0) DIV 1000000000) " s"
57	    println "VERDICT: " passed " PASS, " failed " FAIL of " (passed + failed) (if failed = 0 then " -- ALL PASS" else " -- FAILED" end)
58	    if failed > 0 then fail("MicroGptFlatQuick: " failed " check(s) failed") end
59	  end
60	end

1	# Run C4: the synthesis of rounds two and three
2	
3	C4 is a merge, not a new design. Phase 2 of the C series (`explorations/reviews/run-c2-vs-run-c3.md`, section H) listed what each of the two working programs should take from the other; C4 is those two lists applied to one tree, under the same check and the same goldens, so that the APL side quest has one target program. The decision and its reasons are in `explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md`.
4	
5	## What was merged from where
6	
7	| piece | taken from | why |
8	|---|---|---|
9	| the data side: `FlatData` with the float parser, the loaders, `loadParams(dir, name, count, total)` and the `Corpus` object (`tokens`, `positions`, `valid`, `size`, `length`, `token`) | C3, unchanged but for the header | the keys line of the step names the keys (`ids`, `tg`, `vm`, `pos`) as methods of one object where C2 spelled them as `gather`, `ravel`, `block` and `valid` over two globals; the loader reads the nine files straight into the flat vector, so the model has no load function |
10	| hyperparameters as three untyped tuple bindings | C2 | ledger row 152: a top-level tuple of literals binds; C3's fourteen typed lines were a habit (a binding takes its literal's type). This is also the form the APL sub-language expands a strand assignment to (an APL strand is a Fortress tuple, rung 5), which is what settles it for the target; six untyped declarations to a line, semicolon-separated, also bind (`probes/semicolon`, gap row 175) but have no glyph behind them |
11	| the layout table `matName`, `matShape`, `matCount`, `matOffset`, `nParams`, `view(p, i)` | C2 | `matShape` returns the pair, as Hsu's `SHP` holds pairs; C3's `matRows`/`matCols` is the same table split in two |
12	| `x DOT x` in `rmsn` and `rmsn_b` | C3 | `+/⍵*2` is the dot product; the generator `SUM[t <- x] t^2` is a loop in disguise |
13	| `SUM e` in `sm` | C3 | ledger row 102: `SUM v` parses as a prefix reduction; `BIG MAX` does not and stays a generator |
14	| varargs `flat` | C2 | ledger row 130; C3's nine typed parameters were a habit |
15	| one declaration per elementwise operator, generic in the index type `I` | C2 | ledger row 161: `opr +[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], s: RR64)` serves every rank; C3 had a vector family and a matrix family |
16	| `transpose` as a function beside the postfix `^T` | C2 | a call's result cannot be followed by `^T` (rows 144, 158); `transpose(onehot(…)) dX` reads, `(onehot(…))^T` does not parse; `^T` stays in the model because an api cannot declare an exponent-shaped postfix operator (row 133) |
17	| `diag(v) m` for the loss gradient | C2 | `(vm÷nv)×⍤0 1` is a row scaling; a `Diag` object with its own juxtaposition never forms the matrix; C3's `rows(fn (w, r) => w r, vm / nv, …)` is a lambda for a product |
18	| `x1 wq^T` without parentheses | C2 | postfix binds tighter than juxtaposition; C3's `x1 (wq^T)` was a habit |
19	| the attention block as operators on rank-3 values: `heads`/`unheads` views, `^T` on every plane, the batched juxtaposition, `mask + t`, `rows` over planes | C2 | the target form for the APL round, where `⍤2` over per-head cells is the rank operator over plane views; C3's `cells` lift is faster (1.45× on the check) and is recorded as the alternative, not adopted |
20	| the check: C3's 36 checks plus C2's four single-document losses, 40 in all | both | one file, the same goldens in `explorations/run-c/goldens` |
21	| the tour generator `tour/mktour.py` that checks every snippet against the source | C2 | with its one fault fixed: the inlined SVGs' glyph ids are now prefixed per cell, so the text no longer garbles where two cells share an id (`reviews/run-c2-phase1.md`); the page it writes uses C3's layout (formula and Fortress side by side, Dyalog and note beneath, so the renders stay legible) and the renders take the theme's ink, since dvisvgm's paths carry no colour; C3's page was given the same theme-aware renders |

Nothing was added that neither round had; the semicolon form of the hyperparameter lines was tried after the merge and set aside for the reason in the table.

The step is 20 lines against the Dyalog's 16 (L13 to L28), the difference being the two local views `h` and `u`, the two-line strand of the nine views, and the closing tuple.

42	
43	The tour (`tour.md`, `tour.html`) sets every Dyalog line beside its formula and its Fortress. The lines that differ from C2's are the norms (`x DOT x`), the softmax (`SUM e`), the keys line (the corpus object), the loader (the driver's three lines) and the corpus binding; from C3's, everything from the strand of hyperparameters through the attention block.

45	## The check
46	
47	`src/MicroGptFlatCheck.fss`, 40 checks against `explorations/run-c/goldens` at tolerances 1e-12 on losses and gradients and 1e-8 on finite differences: the loader against P0, the corpus against sixteen golden rows, five batch-1 Adam steps (losses, the step-0 gradient, the weights after Adam, the zero-gradient count), batch 4 (the loss, the four single-document losses, the token-weighted mean), and central finite differences at eleven golden indices for document 0 and for batch 4. Run at pool sizes 1 and 4 (`checks/threads1.txt`, `checks/threads4.txt`): 40 PASS, 0 FAIL, exit 0 in both; 873 s and 396 s; the two outputs differ only in the header's pool size and the timing fields (`diff` after stripping the `( … ms)` fields and the `total` line).

59	C4 costs what C2 costs: on this host C2's re-run (`reviews/run-c2-review-probes/recheck_threads1.txt`, taken under the review's own probe load) and C4 agree to within 8 % on every figure, and the pieces C4 took from C3 (the corpus object, `x DOT x`, `SUM e`) are outside the hot path. C2's own 610 s came from the blinded session's host, which the Phase 1 review put at about 1.5× this one. That also corrects a figure in Phase 2: its "1.45×" for the rank-3 attention set C2's own-host 610 s against C3's this-host 420 s. On one host the rank-3 form costs 2.1× C3's cell lift (8.0 s against 3.7 s per batch-1 step, 873 s against 420 s), the price of the target form for the APL round, paid knowingly. The pool-size-4 figures were taken while nothing else ran; the pool-size-1 run overlapped with the tour work (screenshots and a page rebuild), so its 873 s is an upper bound.
60	
61	## What the type annotations are for
62	
63	Pavol asked whether the model's annotations are necessary, given that the interpreter infers types. The probe (`probes/types`, seven variants of the model with one category removed each) says: only the declared type of a mutable local is required (`p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := …` in the driver; without it the `:=` is not a declaration and `var p = …` is refused, gap row 177). Return types, lambda annotations, the types on the `mask` and `corpus` bindings, the parameter types of the four vector functions handed to `rows` and of the local `h` and `u`, and even the parameter types of the api-declared functions in the component can all be removed at once and the five losses stay identical (rows 176, 178). The model keeps them by choice, not need: the api-declared signatures state the contract where the reader looks for it, and the vector functions' `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` says what a row is. The hyperparameters, which were the annoyance, carry none, in either form.
64	
65	## What C4 settles for the APL round
66	
67	The flat-style program `explorations/apl/reference/hsu-flat/microgpt_concise.dyalog` maps onto C4 as follows, and the program-specific APL design (`explorations/apl/microgpt/DESIGN.md`) starts from this table: `h` and `u` are `heads` and `unheads`; `+.×⍤2` is the batched juxtaposition; `⍉⍤2` is `^T` on an `Array3`; `MK+⍤2` is `mask + t`; `sm⍤1` and `rmsn⍤1` are `rows`; `×⍤0 1` is `diag`; `⌷⍤0 1` is `pick`; `∘.=` is `onehot`; `⊃,/,¨` is `flat`; `v¨⍳9` is the strand of `view(p, i)`; `TOKM[b;]`, `LEN[b]∘.>⍳BLK` and `N⍴⍳BLK` are the corpus object's methods; `⎕NREAD` is `loadParams`; `M∘←`, `V∘←`, `P∘←` are the returned triple of `adam`.
68	
69	Done (2026-09-14, later the same day): `explorations/apl/microgpt/` holds the program in the sub-language and its report; it passes this check at both pool sizes with identical values, at 593 s and 391 s against the 873 s and 396 s above, so the general per-row and per-plane route of the rank operator costs about 1.1× (528 s against 593 s on the restarted container, `checks/rerun-post-restart/`) over the hand-written C4 on this check. What gave at pool size 4 was the frame stack (ledger row 265).
70	
71	## Process
72	
73	Written in the coordinating thread from the two sources in one pass; the merged model compiled and ran on the first attempt (five steps, the losses equal to the oracle's to fifteen digits). Two Opus workers were sent out: one rendered the tour and verified the HTML (the glyph-id check and a by-eye pass over a screenshot); the other was to run the check at both pool sizes, but its run died when the worker stopped to wait on it, six checks from the end, so the coordinating thread ran both checks itself, sequentially, under a monitor that outlives the shell's ten-minute limit. A third worker later gave C2's tour page C4's page section, after Pavol asked for it. No probes were needed for the merge: every mechanism in C4 was already proven in C2 or C3. Two probes followed Pavol's questions: `probes/semicolon` (a ten-second syntax check, run in the thread) and `probes/types` (a worker's seven variants of the model with one category of type annotation removed each). New gap rows: `gaps.md`.

1	<!-- The specification as HTML for a phone: `spec2html.py` converts chapters of `Specification/` (the LaTeX that the revival revises) into the static reader under `docs/specification/`, which GitHub Pages serves at https://palimondo.github.io/fortress/specification/, with the reader's place, notes along the text and their export kept in the browser; a first sample of 2026-11-10 holds the front matter and chapters 1 to 6, and this note says how to run it over more chapters and what does not convert yet. -->
2	
3	# The specification as HTML for a phone
4	
5	`spec2html.py` converts chapters of the specification's LaTeX into a reader of static pages: no server, no external resource, no web font. The pages go to `docs/specification/`, beside the revival page, and GitHub Pages serves them at https://palimondo.github.io/fortress/specification/ once `main` is pushed (`.github/workflows/pages.yml` publishes `docs/`).
6	
7	The first sample holds the front matter (`preface`) and chapters 1 to 6: Introduction, Overview, Programs, Lexical Structure, Evaluation, Types. The contents page lists all 53 chapters and appendices, and marks the 47 that are not converted.
8	
9	## The files
10	
11	- `spec2html.py`: the conversion and the site's pages. Python 3, standard library only.
12	- `reader.css`, `reader.js`: the reader. The build copies them into `docs/specification/`. The colours, the type sizes and the Select button come from the revival page, `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/revival-story.html`. The fonts are the system's: the house fonts are named first in the stacks and used only where a device has them.
13	- `check.js`: the check in Chromium, through Playwright, at a phone's width (below).
14	
15	## Running it
16	
17	From the repository root:
18	
19	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py --list          # every chapter with its slug
20	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py --try variables,functions
21	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py --chapters preface,intro,overview,programs,lexical-structure,evaluation,types,declarations,variables
22	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py                 # the chapters of DEFAULT_CHAPTERS
23	
24	- `--try` converts chapters into the work folder only (`/tmp/spec-html-work/try/`) and prints, for each, the constructs that did not convert. It writes nothing under `docs/`.
25	- A build without `--try` rewrites every page of `docs/specification/`: the chapters named, `index.html` (the contents), `notes.html`, `references.html`, `reader.css` and `reader.js`. To add chapters, add their slugs to `DEFAULT_CHAPTERS` in the script, so that a later plain run keeps them. A cross-reference into a chapter that is not in the list shows its number and the marker "[not converted yet]".
26	- The script exits 1 while a published chapter holds a construct that it did not convert. Such a construct shows in the page in red.
27	- `--base` sets the public address that the links of exported notes start with. `--work` sets the scratch folder.
28	- The script reads `Specification/`, `SpecData/examples/`, `SpecData/tables/` and `Fortify/fortify.el`. It writes nothing in the original tree. It builds and runs no Fortress.
29	
30	After a build, check the pages as a reader sees them:
31	
32	    mkdir -p /tmp/spec-srv && ln -sfn "$PWD/docs" /tmp/spec-srv/fortress
33	    python3 -m http.server 8765 --directory /tmp/spec-srv &
34	    node explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/check.js
35	
36	`check.js` opens every page at 390 px, light and dark, and fails on a page that scrolls sideways. It then writes three notes (a paragraph, a code example, a heading), scrolls, reloads, and checks the notes, the offer to continue on the chapter and on the start page, the export's text, the clipboard, the saved file, a link of the export, edit and delete, an import into a cleared browser, the switch between the two forms of the code, the Select button, that no request leaves the site, and that the pages work when the browser refuses `localStorage`. It saves `spec-reader-light.png` and `spec-reader-dark.png` under `/tmp`. Read the two screenshots: the script does not judge how the text looks.
37	
38	## How the text is converted
39	
40	The script is a converter of its own over the macros that the chapters use. Two tools on this machine were tried first, on Chapter 2:
41	
42	- `pandoc` 3.1.3 (`-f latex -t html --mathml`, with the tree's macro files before the chapter) drops what it does not know without a word. Every `\VAR`, `\TYP`, `\KWD` and `\EXP` of Fortify's markup vanished from the prose ("the type of is inferred"), as did every example, every `\note` and the `\revision` callout.
43	- `htlatex` (TeX4ht, which runs real TeX) stopped at its first use of a superscript under the tree's macros (`! Argument of \:tempc has an extra }`, at `\:tempb{sup}`) and wrote no page. The code environments of `Fortify/fortify.sty` set lines with TeX boxes, which TeX4ht would turn into pictures or lose in any case.
44	
45	What the script does:
46	
47	- **Structure.** It walks the `\input`s from `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` and numbers parts, chapters, sections, subsections and figures as LaTeX does. The chapter numbers agree with the table of contents of `Specification/fortress.pdf`. Each page is one chapter. A section's anchor is its label (`\seclabel{overview:apis}` gives `#sec-overview-apis`), so it stays when sections are renumbered; a section without a label gets `#s-` and its title.
48	- **Blocks.** Every paragraph, code example, table and heading has an id that notes hang on. The id of a paragraph is a hash of its text (`#p-934d16e7`), so it stays while the paragraph's words stay, whatever is added before it. When a revision changes a paragraph, a note on it is kept and listed at the top of its chapter, with the words it was written on.
49	- **Code examples.** An example has two forms, and a switch above it changes all examples at once:
50	  - as the specification renders it. For an example that the build takes from `SpecData/examples/`, the script runs the tree's own tool `foreg` (Fortify, in Emacs, `bin/foreg`) on a copy of the `.fss` file in the work folder, as the specification's `ant genSource` does, and converts the LaTeX that it writes. For an example written by hand in a chapter (`\begin{Fortress}`), it converts that LaTeX. Tab stops become nested boxes, so continuation lines align as in print; a wide example scrolls inside its box.
51	  - as Fortress that a person types: the lines between `(** EXAMPLE **)` and `(** END EXAMPLE **)` of the `.fss` file, or, for a hand-written example, the commented lines that the authors left directly before `\begin{Fortress}`.
52	- **Math and Fortify's markup** become text with Unicode characters, italics, superscripts and subscripts, not pictures and not MathML, so that Speak reads them and a selection copies them.
53	- **Tables and grammar.** `tabular` becomes a table that scrolls inside its box; the `Grammar` environment becomes a box headed "Syntax". The three tables of reserved words, which the build generates with Perl from `SpecData/tables/`, are read from there.
54	- **Cross-references** are links where the target chapter is converted, and the number with "[not converted yet]" where it is not.
55	- **The revival's callouts.** `\revision{label}{text}` becomes a blue box headed "Revised by the 2026 revival", with the reference to its entry in Appendix I. The authors' `\note{}` boxes show as "Draft note", as in a draft build of the PDF.
56	- **Macros.** The `\newcommand`s of `Specification/latex-common/macros/` are read and expanded, so a chapter that uses the tree's own shorthand needs nothing new in the script.
57	
58	## The reader
59	
60	- **Place.** A chapter page stores, in `localStorage` under `fortress-spec.place.v1`, the block at the top of the screen, for each chapter and for the last one read. The start page offers to continue there; a chapter opened from the contents offers the place where that chapter was left.
61	- **Notes.** The pencil at the end of a paragraph, in the bar of a code example, or beside a heading opens a text box under that place. A place with a note has a bar at its left and the note under it, with Edit and Delete. The top of a chapter lists its notes; the bar shows the count; `notes.html` lists all. They are kept under `fortress-spec.notes.v1`.
62	- **Export and import.** `notes.html` shows all notes as text, copies it to the clipboard and saves it as a file. For each note the text gives the chapter, the section's number and title, a link to the place, the kind and first words of the passage, the time, the note's identity, and the note. The same page imports such a file, or its pasted text; a note that is already there is not doubled.
63	- **Without storage** (private browsing, storage switched off) the pages work, a note lasts until the page is left, and a warning says so.
64	- **Select.** The button beside a heading selects that section's text up to its first subsection, for Speak. The list of sections, the buttons and the reader's own notes are not selectable, so they are not read.
65	
66	## What does not convert yet
67	
68	`--try` over all 53 chapters and appendices, 2026-11-10: 33 of the 47 that are not published convert with no construct left over, though nobody has read them at a phone's width yet. The other 14 hold what this table lists:
69	
70	| What | Where | Why |
71	|---|---|---|
72	| The API listings of the library | the library chapters (12 `\input`s of `Specification/library/apis/`) | The build generates them from the library's `.fsi` files with the tree's tool `fortex`; they are not in the tree. The script marks each as "not in this edition". `fortex` is Emacs too, so the script can run it as it runs `foreg`. |
73	| The five drawings of components | chapter 22 (`*.eepic`, 360 drawing commands) | They are pictures in LaTeX's `picture` language; each needs redrawing as SVG. |
74	| Overstruck operator symbols (`\OverStrike`, `\UPTRI`, `\DOWNTRI`) and the operator tables (`\UnicodeOp`, 979 rows, with `\>` tab stops) | chapter 16, appendix F (about 1,300 constructs between them) | The macros build a symbol from two boxes; each needs its Unicode character in the script's table. |
75	| Symbols missing from the table (`\ngeq`, `\preccurlyeq`, `\boxminus`, `\Cap`, `\bmod`, `\binom`, `\genfrac`, `\dddot` ...) | chapters 13, 16, 34, 40, 43, appendix D | One line each in `SYM`. |
76	| `\nolinkurl` (249 uses), `\thinmuskip`, `\lastskip`, `\tracingmacros` | appendix I, chapters 17, 31, 33, 40, 41 | Commands that the script does not know; each is a short handler. |
77	| Appendix A, the calculi | appendix A | The chapter sets its own `\home` and reads four macro files; the script does not follow that yet, and the inference rules (arrays of premises over a conclusion) have no rendering. This is the largest piece of work. |
78	| The bibliography's numbers | every `\cite` | The PDF numbers the cited works (BibTeX, `plain`); the reader cites by key, `[JLS]`, and `references.html` lists every entry of `fortress.bib` under its key. |
79	| The index | every `\index` | Dropped; the reader has no index page. |
80	| Stretching brackets around a matrix, fractions larger than two lines | chapter 2 (two examples), later chapters | The brackets keep their plain size. |
81	| Figures | later chapters | A figure stays where its source is; none floats. |
82	| The source form of a hand-written example without commented source | none in the sample | Such an example shows only as the specification renders it. |
83	
84	The commented source before a hand-written example is the authors' own, and nothing checks that it still matches the LaTeX under it.

#!/bin/bash
# mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads] [full]: the two microGPT checks under walk, each from an empty
# private cache (FORTRESS_CACHES) in a fresh folder under <work-dir> (old runs' folders stay; clear them by hand), each run from its own directory as its header says, both at once,
# with bin/fortress's own JVM (JAVA_FLAGS -Xmx4g -Xss64m) and FORTRESS_THREADS=<threads> (default 1).
# By default the quick pair, MicroGptFlatQuick and MicroGptAplQuick: two forward-and-backward passes each, 7 checks against the goldens,
# timeout 600 s.  With the word full in any position, the full pair, MicroGptFlatCheck and MicroGptAplCheck: 40 checks each, timeout 5400 s.
# Output to <work-dir>/<name>.txt, headed by the machine line (machine.sh) and ended by rc=.
set -u
PROGS="explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlatQuick.fss explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptAplQuick.fss"; LIMIT=600; A=()
for a in "$@"; do
  if [ "$a" = full ]; then PROGS="explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlatCheck.fss explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptAplCheck.fss"; LIMIT=5400
  else A+=("$a"); fi
done
set -- "${A[@]}"
cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../.."                               # $FORTRESS_HOME
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH="/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH" FORTRESS_HOME="$(pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=${3:-1}
W=$(mkdir -p "${1:?usage}" && cd "$1" && pwd)
L=${2:?usage}
for f in $PROGS; do
  (
    t=$(basename "$f" .fss)
    R=$(mktemp -d "$W/run-$t-XXXX"); C="$R/caches"; T="$R/tmp"; mkdir -p "$C" "$T"   # a fresh folder per run; nothing is deleted
    printf '\0\0\0\0' > "$C/global.map"
    {
      bash explorations/compile-ladder/rung-flat-tower/machine.sh "$L $t"
      start=$(date +%s)
      ( cd "$(dirname "$f")" && FORTRESS_CACHES="$C" JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$T" \
          timeout -k 10 $LIMIT "$FORTRESS_HOME/bin/fortress" "$(basename "$f")" < /dev/null )
      echo "rc=$? secs=$(( $(date +%s) - start ))"
    } > "$W/$t.txt" 2>&1
  ) &
done
wait

blocks, or have blocks as parts of the expression, or both (e.g., a while expression is a block, and its body is a different block). See Chapter 13 [not converted yet] for a discussion of expressions in Fortress. In addition, a local declaration begins a block that continues to the end of the smallest enclosing block unless it is a local function declaration and is immediately preceded by another local function declaration. (This exception allows overloaded and mutually recursive local function declarations.) Because Fortress is block-structured, and because the entire program is a block, the smallest block that syntactically contains a program construct is always well defined.

Fortress is expression-oriented: What are often called “statements” in other languages are just expressions with type () in Fortress. They do not evaluate to an interesting value, and are typically evaluated solely for their effects.

Fortress is whitespace-sensitive: Fortress has different contexts influencing the whitespace-sensitivity of expressions as described in Appendix G [not converted yet].

How this edition works A reading edition for a phone: your place, your notes, the code examples, the revival's changes.
  • This is a first sample: 6 of the 53 chapters and appendices are converted. The others are listed below and marked.
  • The page remembers where you stopped, in this browser, and offers to continue there.
  • The pencil at the end of a paragraph, a code example or a heading attaches a note to it. Notes lists them all, and exports them as text.
  • Each code example shows as the specification renders it, and as the Fortress source that a person types. The switch above an example changes them all.
  • A box headed “Revised by the 2026 revival” marks a passage that the revival changed. A box headed “Draft note” is a note of the original authors.
  • The Select button beside a heading selects that section's text, for Speak.
